# Pure-base binding and loss of automatic own-section properness

This note is a bounded status lemma for a positive affine base multiplier.
It does not prove that a jointly minimizing bad family enters, or avoids,
the saturated stratum. It distinguishes a genuine pure-base bottleneck
from partially saturated own cuts and supplies an exact calibration under
all strict closed-minor quotas.

## 1. Exact base-gap criterion using actual compatibility

Let P be finite with positive compatible convex fibers K_z, let the source
(p,y) have y in int K_p, and let Sigma be positive definite. Write

    Gamma(u)=sqrt(u^T Sigma u),       delta=epsilon f(p,y)>0.

The buffered nonvertical cap through this marked source is

    a.(z-p)+u.(X-y)>=-delta Gamma(u).

Let b_base(p) be its weighted closed-halfspace depth on the finite base,
and define the own-fiber circumradius in the covariance metric by

    R(p,y)=max_(X in K_p) sqrt((X-y)^T Sigma^(-1)(X-y)).        (1)

Then the exact alternative is

    b_buffer(p,y)<b_base(p)  iff  delta<R(p,y),
    b_buffer(p,y)=b_base(p)  iff  delta>=R(p,y).               (2)

The converse uses the following actual geometric lemma, suggested and
independently derived by the contributor.

**Whole-fiber capture lemma.** Any ambient CLOSED halfspace H containing
the ENTIRE fiber {p} times K_p has mixed mass at least b_base(p).

Indeed put A={z in P: {z} times K_z is not contained in H}. If A is
nonempty, choose one strict-outside point X_z in every such fiber. If
p belonged to conv(A), an anchored convex representation of p by these
bases would, by actual Minkowski compatibility, put the corresponding
convex combination of the X_z in K_p. Linearity of the strict halfspace
violation would put it strictly outside H, a contradiction. Thus p is
outside the compact polytope conv(A), and a strictly separating closed
BASE halfspace through or containing p excludes all of A. Its selected
fibers are wholly captured by H. Their total mass is at least b_base(p)
and at most the mixed mass of H. If A is empty, the whole mixed family
is captured and the inequality is immediate. Rank-zero is included.

To prove the strict branch of (2), suppose delta<R(p,y). By duality of
the covariance norm there is a Gamma-unit normal u with
min_(X in K_p)u.(X-y)<-delta. Its own cap omits positive d-volume.
Choose an attained atomic base minimizer with normal a_0. For sufficiently
large finite L, the cap with base normal L a_0 has all positive-base-drift
fibers full and all negative-drift fibers empty, because P is finite and
fibers are bounded. Captures on zero-drift fibers are at most their full
masses, and the own zero-drift fiber loses positive mass. The mixed cap
is strictly lighter than the closed atomic cap. In rank zero this is just
the own omission. Hence the strict branch holds.

If delta>=R(p,y), covariance-norm duality instead says that EVERY own
buffered cap is full: min u.(X-y)>=-delta Gamma(u) for every u. The
whole-fiber capture lemma gives mixed mass at least b_base(p) for every
nonvertical buffered cap. The definition also takes the minimum with
the pure-base value, so equality follows. This proves (2).

A useful further consequence is

    b_buffer(p,y)<b_base(p)
       => EVERY active nonvertical cap has a proper own trace. (3)

If an active cap had a full own trace, the lemma would contradict the
strict gap. Its own trace cannot be empty: it contains an open neighborhood
of y because delta>0 and y is interior. Thus it is proper. This replaces
the stronger, unnecessary requirement that ALL directional own cuts be
proper before selecting an active cap.

The old sufficient condition that the whole covariance buffer ellipsoid
be inside K_p guarantees all directional own cuts proper. Criterion (2)
is weaker: it only requires that this ellipsoid NOT contain the entire
own fiber. Actual compatibility then upgrades the gap to (3).

## 2. Arbitrarily small epsilon does not itself prevent pure-base binding

Take d=1, P={-1,0,1}, and K_z=[-1,1] for all three bases. These are actual
compatible constant fibers, with

    M=6,       k=2,       Sigma=1/3.

All strict proper closed-minor quotas hold: singletons have mass 2<3;
two consecutive bases have mass 4<6. There are no other nonempty proper
closed minors. The volume-root compatibility is constant, hence concave.

For any 0<epsilon<=1 put

    q=epsilon^6/2000,
    c=[q(2-q)]^(-1/3),
    ell(z)=c[1+(1-q)z].                                       (4)

This is positive affine on [-1,1] and has geometric-mean normalization

    product_(z in P) ell(z)^(V_z/M)=1,

because ell(-1)ell(0)ell(1)=c^3 q(2-q)=1. The energy at the center of
an interval is E(0)=2. For the aligned invariant buffer

    f(z,X)=[ell(z) E_z(X)/M]^(1/2),

the physical shift at (0,0), using Euclidean unit continuous normal, is

    b=epsilon sqrt(ell(0))/3.

Since q(2-q)<epsilon^6/1000, we have c>10 epsilon^(-2), hence

    b>sqrt(10)/3>1.                                          (5)

Every own cap at (0,0) is therefore full. Let
h(t)=length([-1,1] intersect {X>=t}). For any real tilt a, the cap mass
there is

    h(-b)+h(-b+a)+h(-b-a).

The first term is 2. Monotonicity and the exact identity h(t)+h(-t)=2
show that the remaining two terms sum to at least 2. For |a|>b+1,
one endpoint fiber is full and the other empty, so the mass is exactly
4. The pure-base depth at zero is also 4. Thus

    b_buffer(0,0)=4,       global buffered maximum=4,          (6)

because all marks over zero have pure-base upper bound 4 and both
endpoint bases have pure-base upper bound 2.

All nonvertical minimizing tilts at this displayed mark satisfy
|a|>=b+1. For strict inequality their three fiber statuses are full,
full and empty; at equality the empty fiber has a supporting point.
There is NO proper cut in any of these minimizing caps. In particular
one cannot use the positive proper-coarea inverse solely because
E>0, epsilon is small, or the base quotas are strict.

This is not a bad-depth example: its normalized maximum is 2/3, safely
above Gamma_1/k=1/4. The chosen ell is not a global minimizing ell;
ell=1 gives a smaller maximum for small epsilon. Therefore (4)--(6)
do not refute a possible additional exclusion at an attained JOINT bad
minimum. They identify exactly why fixed-epsilon multiplier compactness
alone does not establish that exclusion.

## 3. Recovering the finite critical-menu interface from a strict base gap

Fix one actual interior source with the strict gap in (2). The usual
finite tilt-compression argument gives a compact set of representatives
for the active nonvertical caps. For clarity, for a fixed Gamma-unit u
classify every fiber as proper, full or empty. On proper fibers its
base drift has a bounded prescribed value. On full or empty fibers it
has one bounded one-sided constraint. The coefficient matrix consists
of the fixed vectors z-p. For each of finitely many status patterns,
the minimum-norm feasible solution is uniformly bounded by the fixed-
matrix polyhedral error bound (or its finite active-set formulas).
Replacing the tilt by that representative preserves every fiber's cap
mass. Normals range over the compact Gamma-unit sphere. The cap mass
is continuous in finite (a,u,c), since u never vanishes and hyperplanes
have zero d-volume in every positive fiber. The infimum is attained.

Every active own cut is proper by (3). There is a UNIFORM positive
properness margin on this compact active set: otherwise a convergent
sequence would limit to an active cap with full own trace, contradicting
the gap. Empty-own degeneration is excluded uniformly by the interior
source and strictly positive delta. Interior section continuity of a
convex body then gives a uniform positive lower bound on the own coarea.
For d=1 the same statement is the constant one-point coarea at an interior
interval cut. No boundary-section continuity is used.

The same conclusion holds for caps with parameters sufficiently close
to this active set and masses/thresholds sufficiently close to the active
ones. Otherwise a compact countersequence would have an improper active
limit. Consequently the right upper quantiles admit exactly the local
strict threshold inverses used in the established buffered construction.
This recovers, locally at this source:

* an attained finite active-normal menu and its concave-envelope balance;
* positive proper own coarea for the exact common-quantile continuation;
* the same full-supergradient/fixed-deepest-face argument for concave f;
* the signed radial supporting-cap directional inverse, whose positive
  proper coarea is now supplied by the active own fiber.

If ALL buffered maximizing marks of a fixed body and multiplier have a
strict base gap, compactness of their finite-base maximizing set makes
these local statements uniform. Interior marks and continuous f follow
from the existing positive-depth/boundary-zero argument. One can then
make the same finite witness selections and exact contact-minimum covers.
The proof does not need a preassigned smallness bound on epsilon ell^(1/N).

Regular differentiability in the full cap parameters is STILL a separate
condition: other fibers can have supporting facets. The existing supporting
branch and allocation theorem, rather than an unproved C1 assertion, must
handle those. The present argument supplies its positive proper coarea;
it does not remove the nonlinear supporting selectors.

## 4. The remaining pure-base stratum

The actual interval calibration in Section 2 lies exactly on the second
branch of (2). Its minimizing caps have no proper coarea, and its atomic
bottleneck cannot be discarded by the strict-gap menu argument. A joint
bad-minimum theorem therefore needs either to show that its maximizing
marks all satisfy the strict branch, or to give a separate argument for
pure-base binding. Fixed-epsilon multiplier compactness alone does neither.

The geometric-mean normalization and quotas alone, without minimizing
information, do not exclude pure-base binding. The explicit example has
all those properties. It is safely above the target and is not a global
parameter minimum, so it does not rule out a stronger consequence of a
hypothetical attained JOINT bad minimum.

## 5. An actual descent for exposed-vertex atomic plateaus

Here is one pure-base stratum that can be excluded without quantile
coareas. Suppose EVERY old buffered maximizing base p in I is a vertex
of conv(P), and its maximum is pure-base-bound. A singleton base halfspace
isolates a vertex, so b_base(p)=V_p. Thus every p in I has V_p=Q, the same
old global raw maximum.

Choose any interior center in each K_p for p in I, and replace those
fibers by their homothetic copies of factor 1-t; keep every other fiber
unchanged. This is an ACTUAL compatible positive family for small t.
An extreme base has no nontrivial anchored representation as target. In
all representations where a modified vertex is an input to another
base, the Minkowski left side only decreases. Thus every anchored
inclusion is preserved exactly, with no hull error.

Put r=(1-t)^d and s=|I|. Then

    V_p(t)=r Q for p in I,
    M(t)=M-s Q(1-r).                                          (7)

The pure-base singleton cap at p bounds the buffered depth of EVERY
new point in its fiber by rQ, regardless of the updated energy or
covariance. The finitely many bases outside I have a strict old maximum
gap. Positive-fiber Hausdorff continuity of buffered depth keeps them
below rQ for sufficiently small t. This uses the actual updated M,
Sigma and multiplier: for example hold the old positive affine ell up
to the scalar

    c(t)=exp[-sum_z V_z(t) log ell(z)/M(t)],

which restores the weighted geometric-mean normalization. This scalar
is continuous and c(0)=1; positivity and affinity are preserved. The
usual all-direction uniform slab estimate therefore applies.

Consequently the actual new global maximum satisfies Q(t)<=rQ, and

    Q(t)/M(t) <= rQ/[M-sQ(1-r)] < Q/M                         (8)

whenever P outside I is nonempty, since then M-sQ>0. This is a strict
physical descent of the normalized invariant buffered objective. It
makes no assumption about a differentiable deepest path.

If I=P, every point of P is a vertex and all weights equal Q. Lattice
completeness then makes their parities distinct: two equally-paritied
vertices would have a new lattice midpoint in P that is not a vertex.
Thus |P|=k and beta=1/k, safely above Gamma_d/k. Therefore an attained
hypothetical bad minimum cannot have only exposed-vertex pure-base
plateaus as its maximizing bases.

This is a solved atomic subcase. It does not cover a pure-base bottleneck
at a nonvertex base, or a mixture of these atomic groups with other
maximizing groups. Shrinking an interior target fiber need not preserve
its active anchored inclusions, and no such freedom is assumed here.
